blocks.text: The **Indus/Harappan Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE)** is famed for the **world's first systematic urban planning** — a **grid layout, standardised baked bricks, the citadel-lower-town division, and an unmatched covered drainage system** — evidence of a highly organised civic authority.

rows: Streets cut at **right angles (N-S / E-W)**; blocks of houses; the earliest 'town planning'.
Raised **citadel** (west) for public/ritual buildings; **lower town** (east) residential; fortified.
**Standardised burnt bricks** in a fixed **4:2:1 ratio**; kiln-fired (unlike contemporaries).
**Covered drains** along streets, house drains connected to street drains, soak-pits, manholes — the finest of the ancient world.
Watertight tank (gypsum mortar, bitumen lining); likely ritual bathing.
Large brick granaries at Harappa & Mohenjodaro — state storage.

blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Grid streets, right angles] --> B[Citadel + Lower town]
  B --> C[Burnt bricks 1:2:4]
  C --> D[Covered drains + soak pits]
  D --> E[Great Bath, granary, Lothal dockyard]

items: Uniform **burnt-brick ratio 1:2:4** and a covered **drainage system** are the two most-tested planning facts.
The **Great Bath** (Mohenjo-daro) = ritual bathing; **granaries** = surplus storage; **no temples/palaces** identified.
Remember the trio: grid streets, standardised bricks (4:2:1), and covered drainage — the exam's favourite IVC facts.
Great Bath (Mohenjodaro), Great Granary, and the citadel/lower-town split are frequent MCQ points.

prelimsPointers: IVC bricks were in a standard **4:2:1 (length:breadth:height)** ratio, **kiln-baked**.
**Great Bath** — at **Mohenjodaro** (citadel); waterproofed with gypsum & bitumen.
Streets ran in a **grid (right angles)**; **covered drainage** with manholes/soak-pits.
**Citadel (west, raised)** + **Lower Town (east, residential)** layout.
**Granaries** — Harappa (near citadel) & Mohenjodaro — state grain storage.
Dockyard at **Lothal**; 'Lower Town' with warehouses; no clearly identified temples/palaces.
Fortifications & the 'Great Granary' show a strong central civic authority.
Grid pattern = **chessboard** layout; houses had private wells & bathrooms.
Dholavira uniquely shows a **three-part** city and elaborate **water reservoirs**.
mainsAngles: Discuss the town planning of the Indus Valley Civilisation as evidence of civic organisation.

glossary.definition: The raised, fortified western mound of a Harappan city housing public and ritual structures.
A large watertight tank at Mohenjodaro, probably used for ritual bathing.
The right-angled street layout of Harappan cities — the earliest systematic town planning.

blocks.text: Harappan society was **urban, seemingly egalitarian and trade-driven**, resting on a **surplus agrarian economy, standardised weights, and extensive internal and long-distance trade** reaching **Mesopotamia (Meluhha)**.

rows: Wheat, barley, peas, sesame, mustard, cotton (**first to grow cotton — 'Sindon'**); ploughed fields at Kalibangan.
Humped cattle, buffalo, sheep, goat; **no conclusive evidence of the horse**.
Bead-making (Chanhudaro, Lothal), shell, metallurgy (bronze — copper+tin), pottery (red-black).
**Binary then decimal** system (16 and multiples); standardised cubical chert weights.
**Steatite seals** (~2000 found) used in trade; Persian Gulf seals abroad.

items: Cotton ('Sindon'), no horse, Meluhha/Dilmun/Magan trade route, and standardised weights are the recurring MCQ facts.
Bead & metal craft centres: Chanhudaro & Lothal.

prelimsPointers: IVC people were the **first to produce cotton** — Greeks called it **'Sindon'**.
**No conclusive evidence of the horse** in mature Harappan sites.
Weights followed a **16-based (binary→decimal)** system; cubical **chert** weights.
Mesopotamian texts call the Indus region **'Meluhha'**; intermediaries **Dilmun (Bahrain), Magan (Oman)**.
**Chanhudaro & Lothal** — bead-making centres; **Lothal** — dockyard (maritime trade).
Metallurgy — **bronze (copper+tin)**; aware of gold, silver, copper, lead; **not iron** (pre-iron age).
Trade was largely **barter**; ~2000 **steatite seals** aided commerce.
mainsAngles: Assess the trade and economic organisation of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

glossary.definition: The Mesopotamian name for the Indus region, evidencing long-distance trade.
The Greek term for cotton, which the Harappans were the first to cultivate.
A carved soapstone seal used in Harappan trade and administration.

blocks.text: Harappan art is **small-scale, realistic and masterly** — the **bronze 'Dancing Girl', the steatite 'Priest-King', terracotta figurines, and the iconic seals (esp. the Pashupati seal)** — reflecting advanced metallurgy (lost-wax casting) and craftsmanship.

rows: Mohenjodaro; three-faced figure surrounded by animals ('proto-Shiva').
The **humped bull** and **unicorn** are common seal motifs.
Mother-goddess figurines, toys, bullock carts; the **'first bronze sculpture' tradition**.

items: Dancing Girl = bronze (lost-wax); Priest-King = steatite; Pashupati seal = 'proto-Shiva' — the three must-know artefacts.
Seals are mostly steatite, square, with the unicorn/humped-bull motif and undeciphered script.

prelimsPointers: **Dancing Girl** — **bronze**, lost-wax (cire-perdue) casting; from **Mohenjodaro**.
**Priest-King** — **steatite** bust with trefoil-patterned shawl.
**Pashupati seal** — three-faced yogic figure with animals; called 'proto-Shiva'.
Seals — mostly **steatite, square**; common motif the **unicorn** and **humped bull**.
Script — **pictographic, boustrophedon (right-to-left first line), undeciphered**.
**Red pottery painted in black**; terracotta mother-goddess figurines.
**Bronze** worked by lost-wax; Daimabad yielded bronze animal figures.
mainsAngles: Describe the artistic achievements of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

glossary.definition: The cire-perdue metal-casting technique used for the bronze Dancing Girl.
A Mohenjodaro seal depicting a yogic, animal-surrounded figure interpreted as a proto-Shiva.
The writing style of the Indus script, alternating direction line by line (first line right-to-left).

blocks.text: Harappan **religion** centred on a **Mother-Goddess, a proto-Shiva (Pashupati), and nature/animal worship**; the **script remains undeciphered**; and the civilisation's **decline (c. 1900 BCE)** is explained by multiple theories — climate/river change being most favoured today.

rows: No monumental temples/idols clearly identified; ritual at the Great Bath.
Mostly **extended inhumation** (N-S); cemetery R-37 (Harappa); pot burials.
**Aryan invasion (Wheeler — now discredited), floods (Mohenjodaro), river drying (Ghaggar-Hakra/Saraswati), climate change/aridity, ecological degradation, decline of trade**.

items: Mother-Goddess + Pashupati + pipal/animal worship = religion; undeciphered pictographic script; multi-causal decline (climate/river most accepted).
Wheeler's Aryan-invasion theory of decline is now largely rejected.

prelimsPointers: Chief deities — **Mother-Goddess** & **Pashupati (proto-Shiva)**; **pipal tree** and **animal (bull) worship**.
Worship of **lingam (phallic) and yoni** symbols is inferred.
**No definite temples** identified; **Great Bath** likely ritual.
Script — **pictographic, ~400+ signs, undeciphered, boustrophedon**; written right-to-left first.
Burials — **extended inhumation** (cemetery R-37, Harappa); some pot/urn burials.
Decline — most-accepted causes: **Ghaggar-Hakra (Saraswati) drying, climate change/aridity, floods**.
**Wheeler's Aryan-invasion** theory of IVC's end is now discredited.
mainsAngles: Examine the religious beliefs and the debate over the decline of the Indus Valley Civilisation.

glossary.definition: The fertility deity represented by numerous Harappan terracotta figurines.
The seasonal river system (identified with the Vedic Saraswati) whose drying is linked to IVC decline.
A Harappan burial site showing extended inhumation practices.

blocks.text: The **Early/Rig Vedic Age (c. 1500–1000 BCE)** was a **pastoral, tribal, largely egalitarian society** of Indo-Aryans in the **Sapta-Sindhu (land of seven rivers)**. Cattle were the measure of wealth; the polity was **kin-based (tribal), not territorial**; and society had **no rigid caste or untouchability**.

rows: **Tribal (jana), not territorial**; chief = **Rajan** (protector of cattle); assemblies **Sabha & Samiti** (and Vidatha, Gana).
**Pastoral & cattle-centred** — cow ('**Gomat**') = wealth; ' **Gavishti**' (search for cows) = war; some agriculture.
**Patriarchal but women respected** (Gargi, Lopamudra, Apala); **no rigid varna/untouchability**; family (kula) basis.
**Nature worship** — **Indra (most hymns), Agni, Varuna, Soma**; yajna (sacrifice); no temples/idols.
**Rig Veda** — oldest (1028 hymns, 10 mandalas); **Gayatri mantra** (to Savitri) in 3rd mandala.

blocks.text: The engine of change was **iron + the plough** — surplus agriculture turned a pastoral tribal society into a caste-stratified territorial monarchy.

items: Cattle-pastoral economy, tribal (not territorial) polity, Sabha/Samiti, Indra-Agni-Varuna worship — the core Rig Vedic facts.
Contrast with the Later Vedic (HC-008): territorial kingdoms, agriculture, rigid varna.

prelimsPointers: Rig Veda — **oldest Veda**; **1028 hymns, 10 mandalas**; books 2–7 the 'family books' (oldest).
Most hymns to **Indra (~250)**, then **Agni (~200)**; **Varuna** = god of cosmic order (rta).
**Sapta-Sindhu** — land of seven rivers; **Saraswati** the most revered river.
Polity **tribal (jana)**; chief **Rajan**; assemblies **Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha, Gana**.
**Cattle = wealth**; war = **'Gavishti'** (search for cows); **Battle of Ten Kings (Dasarajna)** on the Parushni (Ravi).
**No untouchability / rigid caste**; women could attend Sabha; women seers — **Gargi, Lopamudra, Apala, Ghosha**.
**Gayatri mantra** (to Savitri) is in the **3rd mandala** (Vishwamitra).
Early Vedic gods **Indra, Agni, Varuna**; Sabha & Samiti were **real** assemblies; women educated (Gargi, Lopamudra, Maitreyi).
Rig Vedic economy = **pastoral/cattle (gau = wealth)**; 'Gavishti' (search for cattle) = war.
mainsAngles: Contrast the polity, economy and society of the Early and Later Vedic ages.

glossary.definition: The kin-based tribe that formed the basic Rig Vedic political unit, headed by the Rajan.
Rig Vedic tribal assemblies; the Samiti was a larger body that could elect/approve the Rajan.
Literally 'search for cows' — the Rig Vedic term for war, reflecting a cattle-based economy.

blocks.text: The **Later Vedic Age (c. 1000–600 BCE)** saw the shift to the **Ganga plains, iron use ('Krishna Ayas'), settled agriculture, larger territorial kingdoms (janapadas), a rigid varna order, and the rise of elaborate rituals** — the world captured in the later Vedic literature.

rows: **Territorial kingdoms (janapada/rashtra)**; king's power grows (**Rajasuya, Ashvamedha, Vajapeya** sacrifices); Sabha/Samiti decline.
**Iron ('Shyama/Krishna Ayas')**, plough agriculture, rice/wheat; PGW pottery.
**Rigid four-fold varna** hardens; **untouchability & patriarchy** deepen; **four ashramas** emerge.
**Prajapati, Vishnu, Rudra** rise; **ritualism/sacrifice dominates**; reaction later via Upanishads.
**Rig (hymns), Sama (melodies — roots of music), Yajur (rituals), Atharva (magic/charms)**.
Earliest Vedic text, 1028 hymns, praises Indra, Agni
Collection of hymns for rituals, basis of Indian classical music
Procedures for yajnas, divided into Krishna & Shukla Yajurveda

blocks.text: The two civilisations contrasted (a perennial prelims MCQ):

rows: Present-day Pakistan, NW India (Harappa, Mohenjo-Daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan)
Indigenous origin, possibly influenced by Mesopotamia
Polytheistic, worshipped Mother Goddess, Pashupati (proto-Shiva), sacred animals (unicorn, bull)
Nature worship (Indra, Agni, Varuna), later complex rituals (Brahmanism)
No evidence of kings or monarchy; possibly ruled by merchants or councils
Tribal kings (Rajan), later evolved into hereditary monarchy
Well-planned cities, drainage, granaries, Great Bath, citadels
No large cities initially, later simple wood-based houses
Bronze Age civilization (copper, bronze, gold, silver)
Iron Age civilization (iron tools for agriculture, warfare)
No major evidence of warfare, peaceful society
Aryans were warriors, used iron weapons and chariots
Climate change, floods, river shift (Sarasvati drying up), Aryan migration/invasion theory
Town planning, weights & measures, trade practices, possibly influenced Hinduism
Foundation of Hinduism, caste system, Sanskrit texts (Vedas)

items: Iron + agriculture + territorial kingdoms + rigid varna + big royal sacrifices = Later Vedic transformation.
Veda order: Rig→Sama→Yajur→Atharva; Sama = origins of Indian music; Upanishads = Vedanta (end of Vedas).

prelimsPointers: **Sama Veda** — melodies; the **origin of Indian classical music**.
**Yajur Veda** — sacrificial formulae (prose+verse); **Atharva Veda** — spells, charms, medicine.
Royal sacrifices — **Rajasuya (coronation), Ashvamedha (horse), Vajapeya (chariot-race)**.
Iron called **'Shyama' or 'Krishna Ayas'**; **Painted Grey Ware (PGW)** culture.
**Four ashramas** (Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sanyasa) emerge in the Later Vedic period.
**'Satyameva Jayate'** — from the **Mundaka Upanishad**; Upanishads = **Vedanta**.
Each Veda has four parts — **Samhita, Brahmana, Aranyaka, Upanishad**.
**Shruti** = Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads; **Smriti** = Vedangas, Sutras, Epics, Puranas, Manusmriti.
**Samaveda** = roots of Indian music; **Atharvaveda** = spells/medicine; **'Satyameva Jayate'** from Mundaka Upanishad.
IVC = **Bronze Age, urban, undeciphered script**; Vedic = **Iron Age, rural→monarchy, Sanskrit**.
mainsAngles: Trace the transformation from pastoral Rig Vedic to agrarian Later Vedic society.

glossary.definition: 'Black metal' — the Later Vedic term for iron, whose use enabled agrarian expansion.
The horse sacrifice performed by Later Vedic kings to assert sovereignty.
The concluding philosophical texts of the Vedas (Vedanta), exploring Brahman and Atman.
